items.stem: Which of the following historical protests has the strongest continuities with the event shown in the painting?
items.stimulus: The Burning of Jamestown, 1676 “Whereas complaint has been made to this Board by Capt. William Pierce, Esq., that six of his servants and a negro of Mr. Reginald’s has plotted to run away unto the Dutch plantation from their said masters,…the court taking the same into consideration as a dangerous precedent for the future time (if left unpunished), did order that Christopher Miller, a Dutchman (a prime agent in the business), should receive the punishment of whipping,…the said Peter Milcocke to receive thirty stripes and to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R,…said Richard Cockson, after his full time Expired with his master, to serve the colony for two years and a half, and the said Richard Hill to remain upon his good behavior until the next offense, and the said Andrew Noxe to receive thirty stripes, and the said John Williams, a Dutchman and a [surgeon] after his full time of service is Expired with his master, to serve the colony for seven years, and Emanuel, the Negro, to receive thirty stripes and to be burnt in the cheek with the letter R and to work in shackles one year or more as his master shall see cause.” Source: General Court Responds to Runaway Servants and Slaves Minutes of the Council and General Court of Colonial Virginia, 1640
options: The Whiskey Rebellion
The Montgomery Bus Boycott
Nat Turner’s Rebellion
The Bonus Expeditionary Force March on Washington
items.explanation: Correct: (C). The painting depicts Bacon’s Rebellion (1676), when Nathaniel Bacon’s followers burned Jamestown — a revolt of indentured servants and small farmers against the colonial elite, fueled by the labor grievances described in the court record above. Of the choices, Nat Turner’s Rebellion (1831) is the closest parallel: an uprising of bound laborers against the plantation order, met with brutal retaliation. The Whiskey Rebellion was a tax dispute, the Montgomery Bus Boycott a nonviolent civil-rights protest, and the Bonus Expeditionary March a veterans’ compensation protest — none centered on the revolt of servants and enslaved laborers against their masters.

option_explanations.A: The Whiskey Rebellion (1794) was a tax protest by free western farmers, not an uprising of bound laborers against the plantation order.
option_explanations.B: The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-56) was a nonviolent civil-rights protest, not an armed revolt of laborers.
option_explanations.C: The painting shows Bacon's Rebellion (1676) — indentured servants and small farmers burning Jamestown in revolt against the colonial elite. Nat Turner's Rebellion (1831), an uprising of enslaved laborers against the plantation order met with brutal retaliation, is the closest parallel.
option_explanations.D: The Bonus Army march (1932) was a peaceful protest by veterans, not an armed uprising of bound laborers.

items.stem: Why were confrontations such as those in the excerpt rare in the New England colonies?
items.stimulus: The Burning of Jamestown, 1676 “Whereas complaint has been made to this Board by Capt. William Pierce, Esq., that six of his servants and a negro of Mr. Reginald’s has plotted to run away unto the Dutch plantation from their said masters,…the court taking the same into consideration as a dangerous precedent for the future time (if left unpunished), did order that Christopher Miller, a Dutchman (a prime agent in the business), should receive the punishment of whipping,…the said Peter Milcocke to receive thirty stripes and to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R,…said Richard Cockson, after his full time Expired with his master, to serve the colony for two years and a half, and the said Richard Hill to remain upon his good behavior until the next offense, and the said Andrew Noxe to receive thirty stripes, and the said John Williams, a Dutchman and a [surgeon] after his full time of service is Expired with his master, to serve the colony for seven years, and Emanuel, the Negro, to receive thirty stripes and to be burnt in the cheek with the letter R and to work in shackles one year or more as his master shall see cause.” Source: General Court Responds to Runaway Servants and Slaves Minutes of the Council and General Court of Colonial Virginia, 1640
options: New England populations were largely homogenous with economies based on subsistence farming, rather than cash crops.
Puritan law forbade the sale or ownership of enslaved people.
Indentured servants in New England were largely treated fairly, serving for short terms before gaining freedom.
Negotiations after King Philip’s War had ensured the return of indentured servants back to Europe.
items.explanation: The lives of English settlers in New England and the Chesapeake differed considerably. Entire families tended to emigrate to New England; in the Chesapeake, immigrants were often single males. The climate in New England was more hospitable, and so New Englanders tended to live longer and have larger families than Chesapeake residents. A stronger sense of community, and the absence of tobacco as a cash crop, led New Englanders to settle in larger towns that were closer to one another; those in the Chesapeake lived in smaller, more spread-out farming communities.

option_explanations.A: New England was settled by families in town communities with longer lives and no tobacco cash crop, so it never developed the Chesapeake's mass of exploited indentured servants — the labor confrontations of the excerpt's world were rare there.
option_explanations.B: Puritan law did not forbid slavery; enslaved people lived in New England, though in smaller numbers than in the South.
option_explanations.C: Indentured servitude existed in New England as well. The difference was scale and economy, not uniquely fair treatment.
option_explanations.D: King Philip's War (1675-76) ended nothing like this — no negotiation returned indentured servants to Europe.

items.stem: The excerpt best supports which one of the following conclusions?
items.stimulus: The Burning of Jamestown, 1676 “Whereas complaint has been made to this Board by Capt. William Pierce, Esq., that six of his servants and a negro of Mr. Reginald’s has plotted to run away unto the Dutch plantation from their said masters,…the court taking the same into consideration as a dangerous precedent for the future time (if left unpunished), did order that Christopher Miller, a Dutchman (a prime agent in the business), should receive the punishment of whipping,…the said Peter Milcocke to receive thirty stripes and to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R,…said Richard Cockson, after his full time Expired with his master, to serve the colony for two years and a half, and the said Richard Hill to remain upon his good behavior until the next offense, and the said Andrew Noxe to receive thirty stripes, and the said John Williams, a Dutchman and a [surgeon] after his full time of service is Expired with his master, to serve the colony for seven years, and Emanuel, the Negro, to receive thirty stripes and to be burnt in the cheek with the letter R and to work in shackles one year or more as his master shall see cause.” Source: General Court Responds to Runaway Servants and Slaves Minutes of the Council and General Court of Colonial Virginia, 1640
options: English colonists sought to control the native populations through missions and religious conversions.
Trade alliances with Native Americans promoted the economic health of early Chesapeake settlements.
A shortage of indentured servants led to the emergence of the African slave trade.
Chesapeake labor-intensive agriculture used both white and African indentured servants
items.explanation: The excerpt mentions only one of the servants as Negro (Emanuel), so you can logically infer that both white and Black people served in this capacity. Choices (A), (B), and (C) are all unsupported by the excerpt.

option_explanations.A: The court record is about runaway servants and their punishments, not about missions or converting Native peoples.
option_explanations.B: Nothing in the excerpt concerns trade alliances with Native Americans.
option_explanations.C: The excerpt says nothing about a servant shortage causing the slave trade; it simply records the punishments of runaways.
option_explanations.D: The record names six servants plotting escape plus 'a negro of Mr. Reginald's' among them — evidence that Chesapeake labor-intensive agriculture used both white and African indentured servants.

items.stem: The cartoon above supports which one of the following conclusions?
items.stimulus: Illustration created by British publisher William Humphrey, 1783. [Described from the item’s own explanation: a cartoon concerning American treatment of Loyalists after the Revolutionary War. Native American figures stand for the new country — a “savage” land that will not tolerate loyalty to the British Crown.]
options: After the British victory in the Seven Years’ War, many Native Americans sought revenge on British aristocrats.
The French withdrawal from North America after the Seven Years’ War led to various conflicts between Native Americans and colonial settlers.
During and after the Revolutionary War, American sentiment toward those loyal to Britain became increasingly hostile.
Native American warriors were eager to fight alongside American patriots during the American Revolution.
items.explanation: The key to understanding this cartoon is in recognizing the reference to “Loyalists.” Loyalists had no relevance during the Seven Years’ War, so rule out (A) and (B). As for the Native Americans, they are not meant to be taken too literally, so rule out (D). The Native Americans represent the “savage” new country, which will not tolerate loyalty to the British Crown.

option_explanations.A: Britain won the Seven Years' War, and Loyalists — supporters of Britain in the Revolution — are irrelevant to that earlier war.
option_explanations.B: Loyalists are irrelevant to the Seven Years' War period; the cartoon is about the Revolution's aftermath.
option_explanations.C: The 1783 cartoon portrays the new American nation (figured as Native Americans) as a 'savage' land that will not tolerate loyalty to the British Crown — evidence of increasingly hostile American sentiment toward Loyalists during and after the Revolutionary War.
option_explanations.D: The Native American figures are symbolic of the new country, not literal warriors. They are not shown eager to fight alongside patriots.

items.stem: The cartoon above would most likely have found the strongest support among which of the following people?
items.stimulus: Illustration created by British publisher William Humphrey, 1783. [Described from the item’s own explanation: a cartoon concerning American treatment of Loyalists after the Revolutionary War. Native American figures stand for the new country — a “savage” land that will not tolerate loyalty to the British Crown.]
options: A New England craftsman
An Anglican minister
A Pennsylvania farmer desiring western lands
A member of the Virginia House of Burgesses
items.explanation: Since this cartoon is expressing a pro-Loyalist sentiment, pick an answer choice of someone who would be most likely to express that perspective. New England craftsmen tended to be the strongest supporters of the Revolution, so eliminate (A). Pennsylvania farmers were upset that England was preventing them from moving past the Proclamation line, so eliminate (C). The Virginia House of Burgesses supported war against Britain, eliminating (D). Anglican ministers were still strongly tied to England, so (B) is the best answer.

option_explanations.A: New England craftsmen were among the Revolution's strongest supporters; they would not back a pro-Loyalist cartoon.
option_explanations.B: Anglican ministers remained tied to the Church of England and to Britain, making them the likeliest Loyalists — and the likeliest audience for a cartoon sympathetic to Loyalist suffering.
option_explanations.C: Pennsylvania farmers who wanted western lands resented Britain's Proclamation line restricting settlement — they leaned pro-Revolution, not pro-Loyalist.
option_explanations.D: The Virginia House of Burgesses supported war against Britain; its members would not champion the Loyalist cause.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding a cause of the conflict referenced in the cartoon above?
items.stimulus: Illustration created by British publisher William Humphrey, 1783. [Described from the item’s own explanation: a cartoon concerning American treatment of Loyalists after the Revolutionary War. Native American figures stand for the new country — a “savage” land that will not tolerate loyalty to the British Crown.]
options: Britain’s defeat after the Seven Years’ War led to massive debt for the Crown, prompting an effort to collect taxes from the Thirteen Colonies.
Emboldened by their victories during the Seven Years’ War, colonial elites challenged the Crown, pushing for independence before the working-class populace was ready to accept it.
Britain’s massive debt after the Seven Years’ War resulted in a push for greater control over the Thirteen Colonies, sparking debate among colonists over the pursuit of independence.
Disillusioned by their experiences in the Seven Years’ War, colonial militia members formed the Sons of Liberty, a radical group calling for independence from the Crown.
items.explanation: Great Britain’s massive debt from the Seven Years’ War resulted in renewed efforts to consolidate imperial control over North American markets, taxes, and political institutions—actions that were supported by some colonists but resisted by others. Be careful: Britain was not defeated in this war, so rule out (A). Choice (B) is incorrect because many working-class people favored revolution. Choice (D) is unsupportable.

option_explanations.A: Britain was not defeated in the Seven Years' War — it won, which is why it held the empire it then tried to tax and control more tightly.
option_explanations.B: Working-class colonists largely favored revolution; the push for independence was not an elite project imposed on an unwilling populace.
option_explanations.C: Britain's massive Seven Years' War debt drove it to consolidate imperial control — new taxes, tighter regulation of trade and political institutions — which divided colonists and sparked the debate over independence.
option_explanations.D: The Sons of Liberty formed in 1765 to oppose the Stamp Act, not from Seven Years' War militia disillusionment calling for independence.

items.stem: The sentiments expressed by Washington in his Farewell Address most warn against partisan divisions that occurred before which of the following conflicts?
items.stimulus: “…Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. “There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of government, and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true; and in governments of a monarchical cast patriotism may look with indulgence, if not with favor, upon the spirit of party. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged. From their natural tendency it is certain there will always be enough of that spirit for every salutary purpose; and there being constant danger of excess, the effort ought to be by force of public opinion to mitigate and assuage it. A fire not to be quenched, it demands a uniform vigilance to prevent its bursting into a flame, lest, instead of warming, it should consume.” Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796
options: The War of 1812
The Civil War
The Nullification Crisis of 1832
The Korean War
items.explanation: In the excerpt, Washington warns against the “baneful effects” of political parties. During the War of 1812, the War Hawks, largely Democratic-Republicans, saw war as an opportunity to grab new territories to the west and southwest. Their leaders were Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun. Federalists, on the other hand, opposed the war because it disrupted trade. Unaware that its end was coming, they met in Hartford, Connecticut, to consider a massive overhaul of the Constitution or, failing that, secession. When the war ended soon after the Hartford Convention, most people considered the Federalists to be traitors, and their national party soon dissolved. If you chose (B), you were close, but the Civil War involved more than just partisan divisions; it was fueled by geographical, economic, and ideological differences too. Choices (C), the Nullification Crisis of 1832, and (D), the Korean War, were not primarily partisan conflicts.

option_explanations.A: Washington's 1796 Farewell Address warned against 'the baneful effects of the spirit of party.' The first great partisan rupture it foreshadowed came with the War of 1812 — War Hawks versus Federalists, ending in the Hartford Convention.
option_explanations.B: The Civil War's divisions were sectional and came six decades later; the address's warning applied first to the 1812-era party split.
option_explanations.C: The Nullification Crisis (1832) came two decades after the War of 1812's partisan rupture.
option_explanations.D: The Korean War (1950) is a century and a half later — far beyond the address's horizon.

items.stem: Washington’s Farewell Address best exemplifies which of the following political philosophies?
items.stimulus: “…Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. “There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of government, and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true; and in governments of a monarchical cast patriotism may look with indulgence, if not with favor, upon the spirit of party. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged. From their natural tendency it is certain there will always be enough of that spirit for every salutary purpose; and there being constant danger of excess, the effort ought to be by force of public opinion to mitigate and assuage it. A fire not to be quenched, it demands a uniform vigilance to prevent its bursting into a flame, lest, instead of warming, it should consume.” Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796
options: Federalism
Anti-Federalism
Republicanism
Sectionalism
items.explanation: Washington was not explicitly a Federalist, so rule out (A), and he was certainly not an Anti-Federalist, so rule out (B). He preaches against sectionalism, so rule out (D). Washington’s political views most embody Republicanism—which stresses liberty and “unalienable” rights as central values, makes the people as a whole sovereign, rejects aristocracy, expects citizens to be independent in their performance of civic duties, and vilifies corruption.

option_explanations.A: Washington was not explicitly a Federalist; the address is not a Federalist party document.
option_explanations.B: Washington was certainly not an Anti-Federalist; he had presided over the Constitution's creation.
option_explanations.C: The address embodies republicanism: liberty and unalienable rights as central values, the people as sovereign, rejection of aristocracy, citizens' independent civic duty, and condemnation of corruption and faction.
option_explanations.D: Washington preaches against sectionalism, warning of its 'baneful effects' — he does not exemplify it.

items.stem: All of the following features of the Constitution were designed to mitigate the problems described by Washington in the excerpt EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “…Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. “There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of government, and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true; and in governments of a monarchical cast patriotism may look with indulgence, if not with favor, upon the spirit of party. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged. From their natural tendency it is certain there will always be enough of that spirit for every salutary purpose; and there being constant danger of excess, the effort ought to be by force of public opinion to mitigate and assuage it. A fire not to be quenched, it demands a uniform vigilance to prevent its bursting into a flame, lest, instead of warming, it should consume.” Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796
options: the popular election of representatives to the House
the indirect election of senators by state legislatures
the use of an electoral college to select a president
the nomination of judges to the Supreme Court by the executive branch
items.explanation: While all of these are features of the Constitution, you are looking specifically for things that, at the time, would have been believed to limit the influence of partisan politics. In the excerpt, Washington is expressing fear of public opinion becoming dangerous through political parties. Senators being indirectly elected, the use of an electoral college, and selection of judges by the president are all examples of the government not allowing people to directly control the government. Even though from the perspective of 2023, you may know that partisan politics plays into all of those things, at the time the Constitution was believed to limit party politics, except through popularly elected representatives. For that reason, (A) is the best answer.

option_explanations.A: Popular election of House members is the most democratic, partisan-responsive feature of the Constitution — it exposes government to party influence rather than insulating it, so it is the exception.
option_explanations.B: Having state legislatures (indirectly) choose senators was designed to insulate the Senate from popular party passions — a mitigating feature, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Electoral College was designed to filter presidential selection through deliberative electors, limiting direct partisan control — a mitigating feature, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Executive nomination of Supreme Court judges was designed to insulate the judiciary from electoral partisanship — a mitigating feature, not the exception.

items.stem: Which of following Amendments to the Constitution is most directly an example of the sentiments expressed above?
items.stimulus: “Some men look at constitutions with sanctimonious reverence, and deem them like the ark of the covenant, too sacred to be touched. They ascribe to the men of the preceding age a wisdom more than human, and suppose what they did to be beyond amendment…. But I know also, that laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind. As that becomes more developed, more enlightened, as new discoveries are made, new truths disclosed, and manners and opinions change with the change of circumstances, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, 1816
options: The First Amendment, which guaranteed the right to free speech
The Tenth Amendment, which allows powers not granted to the federal government be granted to the states
The Nineteenth Amendment, which guaranteed all women the right to vote
The Twenty-first Amendment, which repealed the prohibition of alcohol
items.explanation: Although all of the Constitutional Amendments represent changes to the original document, the Twenty-first Amendment best exemplifies the sentiment in Jefferson’s quote. After only 15 years of banning alcohol, the Eighteenth Amendment (Prohibition) was repealed by the Twenty-first.

option_explanations.A: The First Amendment (1791) was part of the original Bill of Rights, not a later revision exemplifying Jefferson's point about institutions advancing.
option_explanations.B: The Tenth Amendment (1791) was also part of the original Bill of Rights, not a later change.
option_explanations.C: The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) did change the Constitution, but it extended rights rather than reversing an earlier constitutional choice.
option_explanations.D: The Twenty-first Amendment (1933) repealed the Eighteenth (Prohibition) after only 15 years — the clearest example of institutions 'keeping pace with the times' by undoing an earlier constitutional decision.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a contributing factor in the crafting of the United States Constitution?
items.stimulus: “Some men look at constitutions with sanctimonious reverence, and deem them like the ark of the covenant, too sacred to be touched. They ascribe to the men of the preceding age a wisdom more than human, and suppose what they did to be beyond amendment…. But I know also, that laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind. As that becomes more developed, more enlightened, as new discoveries are made, new truths disclosed, and manners and opinions change with the change of circumstances, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, 1816
options: Individual state constitutions written at the time of the Revolution tended to cede too much power to the federal government, leading to a call for reform on the part of Anti-Federalists.
The weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation led James Madison to question their efficacy and prompted a formation of the Constitutional Congress in 1787.
Difficulties over trade and foreign relations led to a repeal of overly restrictive tariffs required by the Articles of Confederation.
Washington’s embarrassing failure at the Whiskey Rebellion led to Federalist demands for a new framework for federal power.
items.explanation: James Madison led the charge to form a Constitutional Congress and draft the Constitution. It was primarily the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation that led to their rejection. They did not impose tariffs, so rule out (C). Choice (A) is incorrect because the federal government was weak in 1787. Choice (D) is wrong because Washington responded to the Whiskey Rebellion with much force. (If you picked (D), you are confusing Shays’s Rebellion with the Whiskey Rebellion.)

option_explanations.A: State constitutions did not cede too much power to the federal government — the federal government under the Articles was famously weak, not strong.
option_explanations.B: The Articles of Confederation's weaknesses — no tax power, no trade regulation, no executive — led James Madison to question their efficacy and push for the Constitutional Convention that met in Philadelphia in 1787.
option_explanations.C: Congress under the Articles could not impose tariffs at all, so there were no 'overly restrictive tariffs' to repeal.
option_explanations.D: Washington did not fail at the Whiskey Rebellion — he crushed it with federal troops in 1794. Confusing it with Shays's Rebellion (1786-87, under the Articles) gets the history backwards.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the existence of political parties in the early United States?
items.stimulus: “Some men look at constitutions with sanctimonious reverence, and deem them like the ark of the covenant, too sacred to be touched. They ascribe to the men of the preceding age a wisdom more than human, and suppose what they did to be beyond amendment…. But I know also, that laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind. As that becomes more developed, more enlightened, as new discoveries are made, new truths disclosed, and manners and opinions change with the change of circumstances, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, 1816
options: After the drafting of the Constitution, continued debates about states’ rights and competing economic interests led to the formation of political parties, such as the Federalists and the Democratic-Republicans.
Although Washington warned against the influence of political parties, he reluctantly accepted the endorsement of the Federalist Party.
Political parties did not exist until the War of 1812, when Federalists asserted control over foreign policies with France and Britain.
Two major political parties dominated early presidential elections until John Quincy Adams founded the Whig Party in 1824.
items.explanation: Correct: (A). In his Farewell Address Washington warned against political parties, and he remained officially nonpartisan — there was no formal Federalist Party endorsement for him to “reluctantly accept” in 1789/1792, when national parties had not yet formed. The first party system emerged in the 1790s out of post-Constitution debates: Hamilton’s economic program (national bank, assumption of state debts, protective tariffs) and disputes over states’ rights and strict vs. loose construction divided national leaders into Federalists and Democratic-Republicans. Choice (C) is wrong because the Federalist Party collapsed around 1815–1820, after the War of 1812. Choice (D) is wrong because the Whig Party formed in the 1830s in opposition to Andrew Jackson, not in 1824 under John Quincy Adams.

option_explanations.A: The first party system emerged in the 1790s from post-Constitution fights: Hamilton's economic program (national bank, assumption of debts, tariffs) and the clash between states'-rights strict construction and Federalist loose construction produced the Federalists and the Democratic-Republicans.
option_explanations.B: Washington remained officially nonpartisan and there was no formal Federalist Party in 1789/1792 for him to accept an endorsement from — parties had not yet formed.
option_explanations.C: Political parties formed in the 1790s, not with the War of 1812. The Federalists were already declining by 1812, not asserting control.
option_explanations.D: John Quincy Adams did not found the Whig Party in 1824. The Whigs formed in the 1830s in opposition to Andrew Jackson.

items.key_audit_note: Re-keyed 2026-10-01 blind audit: recorded key (B) claimed Washington “reluctantly accepted the endorsement of the Federalist Party” — historically inaccurate; Washington stayed officially nonpartisan and no such party endorsement occurred (national parties barely existed during his elections). Option (A) is the standard, accurate account: post-Constitution debates over states’ rights and competing economic interests produced the Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties in the 1790s. The prior explanation’s dismissal of (A) (“parties existed before the drafting”) was itself false. Explanation rewritten to support (A).

items.stem: Which of the following is a claim made by Jackson in the excerpt above?
items.stimulus: “Is there no danger to our liberty and independence in a bank that in its nature has so little to bind it to our country? The president of the bank has told us that most of the State banks exist by its forbearance. Should its influence become concentrated, as it may under the operation of such an act as this, in the hands of a self-elected directory whose interests are identified with those of the foreign stockholders, will there not be cause to tremble for the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war? Their power would be great whenever they might choose to exert it; but if this monopoly were regularly renewed every fifteen or twenty years on terms proposed by themselves, they might seldom in peace put forth their strength to influence elections or control the affairs of the nation. But if any private citizen or public functionary should interpose to curtail its powers or prevent a renewal of its privileges, it cannot be doubted that he would be made to feel its influence.” Source: President Andrew Jackson, Veto of the Bank of the United States, 1832
options: The existence of the bank is unconstitutional.
The federal government should remove its funds from the national bank and deposit them in state banks.
The national bank concentrates too much power in the hands of the bank’s executive.
The national bank should be regularly renewed every fifteen to twenty years.
items.explanation: While a few of these answers might be true statements, choose one that fits what Jackson actually says. Jackson does think the bank is unconstitutional, but he never mentions that here, so eliminate (A). Similarly, Jackson did take the government’s funds out of the national bank, but that’s not mentioned either, so eliminate (B). Choice (D) uses familiar language from the passage but takes it out of context. Choice (C) provides the best summary of what Jackson says and is the correct answer.

option_explanations.A: Jackson did consider the bank unconstitutional, but he makes no constitutional argument in this passage — the excerpt is about concentrated power, not constitutionality.
option_explanations.B: Jackson did remove federal deposits from the Bank, but this excerpt never mentions moving the government's funds.
option_explanations.C: Jackson's actual claim here is that the Bank concentrates dangerous power 'in the hands of a self-elected directory' tied to foreign stockholders, threatening 'the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war.'
option_explanations.D: The 'fifteen or twenty years' phrase is Jackson's hypothetical about how rarely the Bank would need to show its power if regularly renewed — not his proposal. He opposed recharter entirely.

items.stem: Which of the following events most directly caused the formation of the Second Bank of the United States?
items.stimulus: “Is there no danger to our liberty and independence in a bank that in its nature has so little to bind it to our country? The president of the bank has told us that most of the State banks exist by its forbearance. Should its influence become concentrated, as it may under the operation of such an act as this, in the hands of a self-elected directory whose interests are identified with those of the foreign stockholders, will there not be cause to tremble for the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war? Their power would be great whenever they might choose to exert it; but if this monopoly were regularly renewed every fifteen or twenty years on terms proposed by themselves, they might seldom in peace put forth their strength to influence elections or control the affairs of the nation. But if any private citizen or public functionary should interpose to curtail its powers or prevent a renewal of its privileges, it cannot be doubted that he would be made to feel its influence.” Source: President Andrew Jackson, Veto of the Bank of the United States, 1832
options: The failure of the Specie Circular
Unregulated currency and federal debts after the War of 1812
Efforts by Alexander Hamilton to stabilize the national economy
Federalist counter-reaction to the extreme budget-cutting under Jefferson
items.explanation: In the aftermath of the War of 1812, the federal government suffered from the disarray of an unregulated currency and a lack of fiscal order; business interests sought security for their government bonds. A national alliance arose to create a central bank to address these needs. Choice (C) is tempting, but it refers to the First Bank, not the Second.

option_explanations.A: The Specie Circular (1836) required gold/silver for land purchases — a later Jackson policy, not the cause of the Second Bank's 1816 charter.
option_explanations.B: After the War of 1812 the nation suffered currency chaos — state bank notes of dubious value — plus federal debt. Business and government leaders wanted a central bank to restore fiscal order, producing the Second Bank's charter in 1816.
option_explanations.C: Hamilton's bank was the First Bank of the United States (1791). This question asks about the Second Bank.
option_explanations.D: The Second Bank was not a Federalist reaction to Jeffersonian budget-cutting; it answered postwar financial disarray and was backed by many Democratic-Republicans.

items.stem: The debate over the First Bank of the United States was significant because it raised the issue of
items.stimulus: “Is there no danger to our liberty and independence in a bank that in its nature has so little to bind it to our country? The president of the bank has told us that most of the State banks exist by its forbearance. Should its influence become concentrated, as it may under the operation of such an act as this, in the hands of a self-elected directory whose interests are identified with those of the foreign stockholders, will there not be cause to tremble for the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war? Their power would be great whenever they might choose to exert it; but if this monopoly were regularly renewed every fifteen or twenty years on terms proposed by themselves, they might seldom in peace put forth their strength to influence elections or control the affairs of the nation. But if any private citizen or public functionary should interpose to curtail its powers or prevent a renewal of its privileges, it cannot be doubted that he would be made to feel its influence.” Source: President Andrew Jackson, Veto of the Bank of the United States, 1832
options: whether the new government should issue paper currency
how strictly the Constitution should be interpreted
whether the United States should pay back its war debt to France
whether the president had the power to act unilaterally on important economic issues
items.explanation: As the United States’ first secretary of the treasury, Alexander Hamilton had to handle the nation’s considerable war debt. His solution included the formation of a national bank, modeled on the Bank of England. Through the bank, Hamilton hoped to consolidate and manage the nation’s debt and provide an agency through which a national currency could be circulated. He also wished to broaden the powers of the federal government (Hamilton, a Federalist, favored a strong central government). Both houses of Congress approved Hamilton’s plan, but Washington (then president) was reluctant to sign the bill because he was uncertain of its constitutionality. (Note: Washington performed very conservatively as president, aware that any action he took would set a precedent for his followers. Accordingly, he used his veto only when he was certain that a bill was unconstitutional.) The debate that followed defined the two main schools of thought on constitutional law. On one side were the strict constructionists, led by Jefferson and Madison. Both were wary of a strong central government and interpreted the Constitution accordingly. The strict constructionists argued that the Constitution allowed Congress only those powers specifically granted it or those “necessary and proper” to the execution of its enumerated powers. While a bank might be convenient and perhaps beneficial, they argued, it was not necessary, and thus its creation was beyond the powers of the national government. Hamilton, not surprisingly, disagreed. In his “Defense of the Constitutionality of the Bank,” he proposed what has come to be known as the broad-constructionist view. He argued that the creation of a bank was an implied power of the government because it already had explicit power to coin money, borrow money, and collect taxes. Hamilton argued that the government could do anything in the execution of those enumerated powers—including creating a bank—that was not explicitly forbidden by the Constitution. Washington agreed with Hamilton and signed the bill.

option_explanations.A: Paper currency was not the constitutional question. The fight was over whether Congress could charter a bank at all.
option_explanations.B: Hamilton's bank forced the defining constitutional question of the 1790s: does the 'necessary and proper' clause permit implied powers (Hamilton's loose construction) or only expressly listed powers (Jefferson's strict construction)?
option_explanations.C: Repaying war debt to France was not at issue in the bank debate; managing the debt was, but the constitutional question was about federal power.
option_explanations.D: The debate was about Congress's power to create the bank, not about unilateral presidential power over the economy.

items.stem: The sentiments expressed by Jackson above would have been most shared with which of the following?
items.stimulus: “Is there no danger to our liberty and independence in a bank that in its nature has so little to bind it to our country? The president of the bank has told us that most of the State banks exist by its forbearance. Should its influence become concentrated, as it may under the operation of such an act as this, in the hands of a self-elected directory whose interests are identified with those of the foreign stockholders, will there not be cause to tremble for the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war? Their power would be great whenever they might choose to exert it; but if this monopoly were regularly renewed every fifteen or twenty years on terms proposed by themselves, they might seldom in peace put forth their strength to influence elections or control the affairs of the nation. But if any private citizen or public functionary should interpose to curtail its powers or prevent a renewal of its privileges, it cannot be doubted that he would be made to feel its influence.” Source: President Andrew Jackson, Veto of the Bank of the United States, 1832
options: An oil magnate at the turn of the 20th century
A supply-side economist in the 1980s
A Federalist elected official in the 1790s
A midwestern farmer in the 1890s
items.explanation: In this excerpt, Jackson is critical of the creation of a national bank and expresses a fear that wealthy financiers would unduly control the country’s politics. Since a Federalist elected official created the bank in the 1790s (Hamilton), you can eliminate (C). Supply-side economists in the 1980s saw little problem with economic concentration and generally argued that the wealthy acted as job creators, eliminating (B). Oil magnates like Rockefeller would have been fearful of someone like Jackson trying to regulate their business, removing (A). A midwestern farmer would likely support the Populist movement, which expressed similar skepticism toward banks, so (D) is the best choice.

option_explanations.A: Oil magnates like Rockefeller embodied the concentrated wealth Jackson warned against — they would fear Jackson's attack, not share it.
option_explanations.B: 1980s supply-side economists celebrated concentrated wealth as job-creating; they saw no problem with economic concentration.
option_explanations.C: 1790s Federalist officials — Hamilton's allies — created the national bank Jackson was attacking.
option_explanations.D: Midwestern farmers of the 1890s — the Populist base — shared Jackson's suspicion that wealthy eastern financiers and banks controlled the country's politics against ordinary producers.

items.stem: Which of the following describes an effect of the policy enacted by Jackson above?
items.stimulus: “Is there no danger to our liberty and independence in a bank that in its nature has so little to bind it to our country? The president of the bank has told us that most of the State banks exist by its forbearance. Should its influence become concentrated, as it may under the operation of such an act as this, in the hands of a self-elected directory whose interests are identified with those of the foreign stockholders, will there not be cause to tremble for the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war? Their power would be great whenever they might choose to exert it; but if this monopoly were regularly renewed every fifteen or twenty years on terms proposed by themselves, they might seldom in peace put forth their strength to influence elections or control the affairs of the nation. But if any private citizen or public functionary should interpose to curtail its powers or prevent a renewal of its privileges, it cannot be doubted that he would be made to feel its influence.” Source: President Andrew Jackson, Veto of the Bank of the United States, 1832
options: A nationally integrated market system connected by canals and rail was created.
A new political party system was formed.
A stable, resilient system of state and local banks was reinforced.
An amendment limiting the president’s veto power was enacted.
items.explanation: This question is asking us about an effect of Jackson’s bank war. Even though a nationally integrated market system developed in this time, it wasn’t a consequence of this policy. The system of state and local banks was hardly resilient as a major economic panic happened in 1837 partly due to Jackson’s “pet bank” policies, so eliminate (C). Though critics likely would have wanted to limit Jackson’s veto power, this never happened, eliminating (D). Choice (B) is the best answer because Jackson’s policies helped create a new party system with the Whigs as his opponents.

option_explanations.A: The market revolution's canals and rails developed independently of the Bank War; they were not its product.
option_explanations.B: The Bank War polarized the nation and helped crystallize the Second Party System: Jackson's Democrats versus the Whigs, who formed in opposition to 'King Andrew' and his financial policies.
option_explanations.C: The 'pet bank' system was not stable or resilient — its reckless lending helped trigger the Panic of 1837.
option_explanations.D: No amendment limiting the veto was ever enacted; Jackson's vigorous use of the veto stood.

items.stem: Supreme Court decisions concerning Native American tribes in 1831 and 1832 did which of the following?
items.stimulus: Map From 1830
options: reinforced the rights of states to remove Native Americans from disputed lands
denied them the right to sue in federal court but affirmed their rights to land that was traditionally theirs
voided previous treaties between Native American tribes and the United States on the grounds that the treaties were unfair
ruled that the federal government had a unilateral right to relocate Native Americans to lands west of the Mississippi
items.explanation: In the 1831 case Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that Native American tribes were neither foreign nations nor states, and as such had no standing in federal court. In short, he ruled they had no right to sue. He argued further, however, that the tribes had a right to their lands and could not be forced to give them up by anyone, including the federal government. The 1832 case Worcester v. Georgia reaffirmed that position.

option_explanations.A: Marshall did not reinforce states' removal rights. Worcester v. Georgia (1832) limited Georgia's authority over Cherokee lands.
option_explanations.B: In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) Marshall held tribes were 'domestic dependent nations' — neither foreign nations nor states — with no standing to sue as such. But he affirmed they held rights to their traditional lands that no one, including the federal government, could take by force; Worcester (1832) reaffirmed it.
option_explanations.C: The decisions did not void treaties as unfair; they addressed tribal legal status and land rights.
option_explanations.D: Marshall granted no unilateral federal relocation power; he affirmed tribal land rights against forced taking.

items.stem: Which of the following factors are most likely to have caused the migration shown in the map above?
items.stimulus: Map From 1830
options: Federal executive branch mandates
Supreme Court judicial decisions
Legislative incentives for homesteading in the West
State legislative mandates for Native American removal
items.explanation: As noted above, it was President Jackson who was largely responsible for relocating the Cherokees, not the Supreme Court or the Legislature.

option_explanations.A: The migration shown is the Cherokee removal, driven by President Jackson's executive enforcement of the Indian Removal Act (1830) — federal executive mandates, carried out despite the Supreme Court's objections.
option_explanations.B: Supreme Court decisions (Worcester v. Georgia) opposed removal; they did not cause the migration.
option_explanations.C: Homesteading incentives like the 1862 Homestead Act came decades later and concerned western settlement, not 1830s Cherokee removal.
option_explanations.D: State legislatures (Georgia's) pressured for removal, but the migration itself was executed by federal authority, not state mandate.

items.stem: All of the following events can be understood as consequences of the policy illustrated above EXCEPT
items.stimulus: Map From 1830
options: the Trail of Tears
King Philip’s War
Creek War of 1836
the Battle of Little Big Horn
items.explanation: King Philip’s War was an armed conflict between the Indigenous inhabitants of present-day New England and English colonists. The war is named after the Wampanoag chief, Metacomet, known to the English as “King Philip.” This war is least like the migration depicted in the map—the Cherokee Trail of Tears, as in (A)—because it did not lead to a forced migration. King Phillip’s warriors prevailed over the short term. Choice (D), the Battle of Little Big Horn, is a tempting answer, but ultimately the Lakota Sioux were forced to leave their territories and migrate to reservations. The Creek War of 1836, (C), was directly associated with the forced relocation of the Creek Nation westward as represented on the map.

option_explanations.A: The Trail of Tears — the forced Cherokee march west — was the direct consequence of the removal policy shown, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: King Philip's War (1675-76) was a 17th-century New England conflict, more than 150 years before the removal policy. It is the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Creek War of 1836 (the Second Creek War) arose from removal enforcement — a consequence, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Battle of Little Bighorn (1876) was part of the long chain of Plains wars flowing from removal-and-reservation policy — a consequence, not the exception.

items.stem: In the late 1800s, federal policy toward Native Americans shifted from that shown above to
items.stimulus: Map From 1830
options: a recognition of equal Native American sovereignty
attempts to assimilate Native Americans through individual land grants
establishment of land reservations for Indigenous tribes
granting of American citizenship to Native groups
items.explanation: The establishment of reservations was being reflected already in the image above, so that hardly represents a change. Eliminate (C). The United States was hardly interested in granting American citizenship to Native groups or granting them any kind of equal sovereignty in the 1800s, eliminating (A) and (D). The United States did attempt to assimilate Native Americans with the Dawes Act in 1887, so (B) is the best answer.

option_explanations.A: The United States never recognized equal Native sovereignty in the 1800s; that was never the policy shift.
option_explanations.B: The Dawes Act (1887) broke tribal lands into individual allotments to force assimilation — farming, private property, 'civilization' — replacing removal with a policy of cultural absorption.
option_explanations.C: Reservations were the existing policy of the removal era shown in the map, not the new direction.
option_explanations.D: Broad Native citizenship did not come in the late 1800s (the Indian Citizenship Act was 1924); it was not the policy shift.

items.stem: Which of the following was an immediate consequence of the secession of South Carolina?
items.stimulus: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that…a war must be waged against slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States. “The guaranties of the Constitution will then no longer exist; the equal rights of the States will be lost. The slave-holding States will no longer have the power of self-government, or self-protection, and the Federal Government will have become their enemy. “Sectional interest and animosity will deepen the irritation, and all hope of remedy is rendered vain, by the fact that public opinion at the North has invested a great political error with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. We, therefore, the People of South Carolina…have solemnly declared that the Union heretofore existing between this State and the other States of North America, is dissolved, and that the State of South Carolina has resumed her position among the nations of the world, as a separate and independent State.” Source: “Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union,” 1860
options: Southern Democrats appealed to the powers of Congress to stop military action against South Carolina.
Abraham Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation.
Other southern states seceded from the Union, forming the Confederacy.
Jefferson Davis drafted Confederate soldiers into war, defending the siege on Fort Sumter.
items.explanation: This is a question of chronology. There was no Confederacy until South Carolina seceded first, so rule out (D). By the time the Civil War started, Southern Democrats appealed more to Jefferson Davis than to Washington, D.C., so rule out (A). Lincoln did not sign the Emancipation Proclamation until much later in the war, so rule out (B).

option_explanations.A: After secession, Southern Democrats looked to Jefferson Davis and Richmond, not to Congress in Washington, to stop military action.
option_explanations.B: Lincoln did not sign the Emancipation Proclamation until January 1863 — two years after South Carolina seceded.
option_explanations.C: South Carolina seceded in December 1860; six more states followed and formed the Confederacy in February 1861 — the immediate consequence.
option_explanations.D: There was no Confederacy until after South Carolina seceded, and Fort Sumter was not attacked until April 1861 — this option scrambles the chronology.

items.stem: The sentiments above are most consistent with which of the following ideologies?
items.stimulus: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that…a war must be waged against slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States. “The guaranties of the Constitution will then no longer exist; the equal rights of the States will be lost. The slave-holding States will no longer have the power of self-government, or self-protection, and the Federal Government will have become their enemy. “Sectional interest and animosity will deepen the irritation, and all hope of remedy is rendered vain, by the fact that public opinion at the North has invested a great political error with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. We, therefore, the People of South Carolina…have solemnly declared that the Union heretofore existing between this State and the other States of North America, is dissolved, and that the State of South Carolina has resumed her position among the nations of the world, as a separate and independent State.” Source: “Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union,” 1860
options: States’ rights
Nullification
Neutrality
Civil disobedience
items.explanation: While the key concerns of South Carolina toward maintaining slavery were a driving force behind secession, the rationale for secession provided in this excerpt is a violation of “the equal rights of the states” as provided by the Constitution. Choice (B), nullification, is a plausible but incorrect choice: South Carolina did attempt to nullify a tariff under President Jackson (the Tariff of Abominations, 1828 — not the Whiskey Tax), but the excerpt's rationale is constitutional equal rights of the states. Choice (D), civil disobedience, cannot be right because that sort of protest is nonviolent in nature.

option_explanations.A: The excerpt justifies secession as defense of 'the equal rights of the States' under the Constitution — the states'-rights rationale: the federal government had become the slave states' enemy.
option_explanations.B: Nullification was South Carolina's 1832 tactic against the tariff — a related doctrine, but this excerpt argues secession, not nullification of a law within the Union.
option_explanations.C: Neutrality has nothing to do with secession; South Carolina was taking a revolutionary break, not a neutral stance.
option_explanations.D: Civil disobedience is nonviolent protest within a system. Secession was a complete break from the Union, not disobedience within it.

items.stem: In the excerpt above, the reference to “the sanction of more erroneous religious belief” most probably refers to
items.stimulus: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that…a war must be waged against slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States. “The guaranties of the Constitution will then no longer exist; the equal rights of the States will be lost. The slave-holding States will no longer have the power of self-government, or self-protection, and the Federal Government will have become their enemy. “Sectional interest and animosity will deepen the irritation, and all hope of remedy is rendered vain, by the fact that public opinion at the North has invested a great political error with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. We, therefore, the People of South Carolina…have solemnly declared that the Union heretofore existing between this State and the other States of North America, is dissolved, and that the State of South Carolina has resumed her position among the nations of the world, as a separate and independent State.” Source: “Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union,” 1860
options: Southern Baptist justification of slavery on the grounds of white racial superiority
the Puritan abolition of slavery in New England states
Jewish slavery in the Torah
Christian abolitionist rejection of slavery on moral grounds
items.explanation: The Quakers believed slavery to be morally wrong and argued for its end. More generally, the religious and moral fervor that accompanied the Second Great Awakening persuaded many white Northerners that slavery was a great evil. Southern Baptists, (A), were not abolitionists at all — they defended slavery (the denomination split from northern Baptists in 1845 over slaveholding missionaries). Puritans disapproved of slavery, as in (B), but they did not successfully ban it from the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Choice (C) is irrelevant to this question.

option_explanations.A: Southern Baptists defended slavery; they were not the Northern religious opinion South Carolina denounces as 'erroneous.'
option_explanations.B: Puritans did not abolish slavery in New England (it existed there), and they are not the 1860 Northern religious force the excerpt means.
option_explanations.C: Slavery in the Torah is irrelevant to Northern public opinion in 1860.
option_explanations.D: South Carolina means Northern Christian abolitionism — the Second Great Awakening-fueled moral condemnation of slavery by Quakers and evangelicals — which it dismisses as 'erroneous religious belief.'

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why South Carolina chose to secede from the Union in 1860?
items.stimulus: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that…a war must be waged against slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States. “The guaranties of the Constitution will then no longer exist; the equal rights of the States will be lost. The slave-holding States will no longer have the power of self-government, or self-protection, and the Federal Government will have become their enemy. “Sectional interest and animosity will deepen the irritation, and all hope of remedy is rendered vain, by the fact that public opinion at the North has invested a great political error with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. We, therefore, the People of South Carolina…have solemnly declared that the Union heretofore existing between this State and the other States of North America, is dissolved, and that the State of South Carolina has resumed her position among the nations of the world, as a separate and independent State.” Source: “Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union,” 1860
options: The failures of the Compromise of 1850 hindered South Carolina’s trade relationships with Western states, leading to severe economic recession.
The Battle of Fort Sumter occurred in Charleston, prompting public outrage over Union aggression.
President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation, thus undermining slavery in the South.
Lincoln’s election on a Free-Soil platform led southern politicians to conclude that secession was necessary.
items.explanation: Again, this is an issue of chronology. Choices (B) and (C) occurred after South Carolina’s secession. Trade issues, as in (A), were not a primary reason for South Carolina’s exit.

option_explanations.A: Trade troubles from the Compromise of 1850 were not South Carolina's reason for seceding; the trigger was political, not commercial.
option_explanations.B: The Battle of Fort Sumter (April 1861) happened after secession (December 1860) — it cannot explain it.
option_explanations.C: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) came more than two years after secession — it cannot explain it.
option_explanations.D: Lincoln's 1860 election on the Free-Soil platform — opposing slavery's expansion — convinced Southern leaders that the federal government would become, in the excerpt's words, 'their enemy,' making secession necessary.

items.stem: The sentiment expressed by Beveridge best exemplifies which of the following?
items.stimulus: “The Opposition tells us that we ought not to govern a people without their consent. I answer, the rule of liberty that all just government derives its authority from the consent of the governed, applies only to those who are capable of self-government. We govern the Indians without their consent, we govern our territories without their consent, we govern our children without their consent. How do they know that our government would be without their consent? Would not the people of the Philippines prefer the just, human, civilizing government of this Republic to the savage, bloody rule of pillage and extortion from which we have rescued them? And, regardless of this formula of words made only for enlightened, self-governing people, do we owe no duty to the world? Shall we turn these peoples back to the reeking hands from which we have taken them? Shall we abandon them, with Germany, England, Japan, hungering for them? Shall we save them from those nations, to give them a self-rule of tragedy?…Then like men and not like children, let us on to our tasks, our mission, and our destiny.” Source: Albert J. Beveridge, “The March of the Flag,” 1898
options: Imperialism
Anti-imperialism
Isolationism
Manifest Destiny
items.explanation: In the excerpt, Beveridge is arguing that America is justified in ruling over less-developed nations with or without their consent but that those nations would surely appreciate the “just, human, civilizing” influence of the West. These sentiments are the hallmarks of Imperialism. Choice (D), Manifest Destiny, pertains more to domestic expansion, rather than international affairs.

option_explanations.A: Beveridge argues America is justified in governing 'less-developed nations' without their consent because they are 'incapable of self-government' — the classic rationale of imperialism.
option_explanations.B: Anti-imperialists (the Anti-Imperialist League) opposed exactly this argument; Beveridge is answering them, not joining them.
option_explanations.C: Isolationism opposes overseas engagement. Beveridge demands it as a duty.
option_explanations.D: Manifest Destiny concerned continental expansion within North America; Beveridge is justifying overseas empire in the Philippines.

items.stem: The United States became politically engaged with the Philippines after what military conflict?
items.stimulus: “The Opposition tells us that we ought not to govern a people without their consent. I answer, the rule of liberty that all just government derives its authority from the consent of the governed, applies only to those who are capable of self-government. We govern the Indians without their consent, we govern our territories without their consent, we govern our children without their consent. How do they know that our government would be without their consent? Would not the people of the Philippines prefer the just, human, civilizing government of this Republic to the savage, bloody rule of pillage and extortion from which we have rescued them? And, regardless of this formula of words made only for enlightened, self-governing people, do we owe no duty to the world? Shall we turn these peoples back to the reeking hands from which we have taken them? Shall we abandon them, with Germany, England, Japan, hungering for them? Shall we save them from those nations, to give them a self-rule of tragedy?…Then like men and not like children, let us on to our tasks, our mission, and our destiny.” Source: Albert J. Beveridge, “The March of the Flag,” 1898
options: Mexican–American War
World War II
Spanish–American War
The Boxer Rebellion
items.explanation: During the Spanish–American War, the United States not only drove Spain out of Cuba but also sent a fleet to the Spanish-controlled Philippines and drove the Spanish out of there too. In the Treaty of Paris, Spain granted Cuba independence and ceded the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Guam to the United States.

option_explanations.A: The Mexican-American War (1846-48) won the Southwest, not the Philippines.
option_explanations.B: World War II (1941-45) came four decades after the United States first took the Philippines.
option_explanations.C: In the Spanish-American War (1898), Dewey's fleet took Manila Bay, and the Treaty of Paris ceded the Philippines (with Puerto Rico and Guam) to the United States — the start of American engagement there.
option_explanations.D: The Boxer Rebellion (1900) was in China and transferred no territory to the United States.

items.stem: Which of the following rationales does Beveridge employ in his argument?
items.stimulus: “The Opposition tells us that we ought not to govern a people without their consent. I answer, the rule of liberty that all just government derives its authority from the consent of the governed, applies only to those who are capable of self-government. We govern the Indians without their consent, we govern our territories without their consent, we govern our children without their consent. How do they know that our government would be without their consent? Would not the people of the Philippines prefer the just, human, civilizing government of this Republic to the savage, bloody rule of pillage and extortion from which we have rescued them? And, regardless of this formula of words made only for enlightened, self-governing people, do we owe no duty to the world? Shall we turn these peoples back to the reeking hands from which we have taken them? Shall we abandon them, with Germany, England, Japan, hungering for them? Shall we save them from those nations, to give them a self-rule of tragedy?…Then like men and not like children, let us on to our tasks, our mission, and our destiny.” Source: Albert J. Beveridge, “The March of the Flag,” 1898
options: The closing of the western frontier impels the United States to expand its territory overseas.
Governing territories confers economic benefits to both European and non-white nations.
Powerful nations have a moral duty to govern less-developed nations.
Racial superiority confers responsibility to the United States and Europe over the affairs of developing nations.
items.explanation: Beveridge uses largely moral arguments, stating that less-developed nations must be “rescued” from “the savage, bloody rule of pillage and extortion.” There is no mention of economic benefits, or racial superiority, so rule out (B) and (D), respectively. Choice (A) is describing Manifest Destiny, not Progressive Imperialism.

option_explanations.A: The closing of the western frontier is Frederick Jackson Turner's thesis about domestic expansion, not Beveridge's argument here.
option_explanations.B: Beveridge mentions no economic benefits to either side. His case is entirely moral — rescue and civilization.
option_explanations.C: Beveridge's core rationale is moral duty: America owes 'duty to the world' to govern peoples he deems incapable of self-government, rescuing them from 'savage, bloody rule' with 'just, human, civilizing government.'
option_explanations.D: Beveridge does not explicitly argue racial superiority in this passage; the rationale he actually employs is moral duty and the civilizing mission.
